newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOXING-JAPAN GETS RICHER, THE SPORT GETS POORER.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-JAPAN GETS RICHER, THE SPORT GETS POORER.

text.p: Money has lured many a man into the boxing ring but in Japan wealth is being blamed for a decline in the number of top-level fighters.
There was a time when the country could consider itself a genuine world power in the lighter divisions of boxing.
No more. Japan lost its last world title in February when World Boxing Council (WBC) super flyweight champion Hiroshima Kawashima lost on a split decision to Filipino Gerry Penalosa.
Although there are 2,500 professional boxers training in 200 superbly-equipped gyms, nobody is forecasting a Japanese champion soon in any of the 34 titles up for grabs in the world.
The problem seems partly to be that the Japanese are simply too well-off to fight for a living.

One of Japan's leading sports writers, Hiro Otaka of the Asahi Shimbun, said Japan's top champions over the past 40 years came mainly from poor backgrounds and went into the ring as hungry youngsters.
"There's no such poverty and hunger in Japan in recent years to bring out the best fighters," he said.
It is a cycle in boxing that repeats itself.

In the pre-war period, many top U.S. boxers were Jewish, Italians and Irish from poor urban ghettos. As their social fortunes improved, the ring was taken over by black boxers from similar backgrounds.

In the lower weights, the hungry and unemployed of Thailand, Mexico and the Philippines have come to dominate rankings where Japan once had its share of champions. Thailand boasts six world champions.
One of the best-loved Japanese boxing champions was Yoshio Shirai (48-8-2, 20 KOs) who took the flyweight title from Dado Marino of the United States in 1952.
That was a first for Japan, with the ex-factory worker developing a great boxing technique and defending his title four times.
Masahiko "Fighting" Harada (36-7, 23 KOs) took the flyweight title in 1962 and went on after three years to grab the bantamweight world honours from Brazilian Eder Jofre.
Junior flyweight Yoko Gushiken (23-1,15 KOs) who defended his world title from 1976-81, was a strong southpaw who came from a poor rural background in Okinawa.
There have been 39 Japanese holders of world titles since Shirai first set the pattern.
The home-grown champions may be thin on the ground now but the fans can still cheer two locally-based world champions who fight regularly out of Japan.

WBC featherweight champion Luisito Espinosa of the Philippines and WBA flyweight champion Yuri Arbachakov of Russia are happy to be based in Japan and earn far more money than they would in their own countries.
Okinawa Makoto, an assistant manager at one Japanese gym, rated the country's chances of having a world champion in the near future as "about evens".
In Yokohama, on Saturday, two Japanese boxers on the bill will be cheered on in world title fights.

Yuichi Kasai will try to outbox Antonio Cermeno of Venezuela for the WBA junior featherweight title and Steve Johnson of the U.S. will defend his WBC lightweight title against Japan's Hiroyuko Sakamoto.
"It will be a big night for Japanese boxing," said Makoto.

If the pair of hopefuls fail, then in October the WBA junior lightweight title fight in Tokyo between champion Choi Young-soo and challenger Takano Hatakeyama will provide a thrilling battle between ancient adversaries: Korea and Japan.

The secretary general of the Japan Boxing Commission, Shigeru Kojima, said: "We need a champion so that other young boxers will aim for such honours. It's not comfortable to know that Thailand has six and we have none."
